title: SQL and JPQL Injection in Statement Execution
platform_conditions: Java SE 8+ (JDBC java.sql / javax.persistence JPQL); applies to any JDBC driver and JPA provider
security_mechanism: java.sql.Statement executes the string exactly as passed, so ' + id + ' concatenation composes the value into the SQL text before the database parses it; PreparedStatement instead sends the statement and parameters separately and the driver binds them after parsing, making the boundary structural rather than escaper-dependent. JPQL/SQL via EntityManager.createQuery or createNativeQuery has the same split: named/positional parameters (:id, ?1) are bound out-of-band, while string concatenation lets a quote in the value become query syntax. ORDER BY, table, and column names cannot be parameterized anywhere, so they must come from a server-side allowlist, never from client text.

source_sink_clues.source: Request parameters, filter/sort field names from the client, and values concatenated into Statement or JPQL strings.
source_sink_clues.sink: Statement.executeQuery/executeUpdate with concatenated SQL; EntityManager.createQuery/createNativeQuery with string concatenation; any raw-SQL helper composing ORDER BY or identifier fragments from input

tracking_guards: Require PreparedStatement with ? placeholders and setString/setInt (or JPA parameter binding via setParameter) for every value; require non-parameterizable identifiers be mapped through a fixed allowlist dictionary from client keys to server-side constants; treat any concatenation in the query string as a candidate.
not_candidate_when: All values bind through PreparedStatement or JPA parameter binding, the only concatenated fragments come from a fixed server-side mapping, or the query string is a constant and parameters carry all dynamics.
synthetic_vulnerable_example: stmt.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = '" + id + "'");
synthetic_safe_example: PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = ?"); ps.setString(1, id);
public_references: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in SQL Command — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html
